playground.label: Project 5: back up a folder into numbered ZIP files (temporary folder, no input)
playground.code:
import os, shutil, tempfile, zipfile
from pathlib import Path

root = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
spam = root / 'spam'
(spam / 'eggs').mkdir(parents=True)
(spam / 'file1.txt').write_text('Hello')
(spam / 'eggs' / 'file2.txt').write_text('Hello' * 100)
os.chdir(root)

def backup_to_zip(folder):
    folder = Path(folder)
    number = 1
    while True:
        zip_filename = Path(folder.parts[-1] + '_' + str(number) + '.zip')
        if not zip_filename.exists():
            break
        number = number + 1
    print(f'Creating {zip_filename}...')
    with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_filename, 'w', zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as backup_zip:
        for folder_name, subfolders, filenames in os.walk(folder):
            subfolders.sort()
            filenames.sort()
            folder_name = Path(folder_name)
            print(f'Adding files in folder {folder_name.relative_to(root)}...')
            for filename in filenames:
                print(f'Adding file {filename}...')
                path = folder_name / filename
                backup_zip.write(path, arcname=path.relative_to(root))
    print('Done.')

backup_to_zip(spam)
backup_to_zip(spam)
print(sorted(zipfile.ZipFile('spam_2.zip').namelist()))
os.chdir('/')
shutil.rmtree(root)

findings: Chapter 11 of the 3rd edition, Organizing Files, teaches the shutil module with shutil.copy(), shutil.copytree() and shutil.move() for copying, moving and renaming; permanent deletion with os.unlink(), os.rmdir() and shutil.rmtree(), with a dry run as protection and the third-party send2trash module as the recoverable alternative; listing a folder with os.listdir() and iterdir() and walking a tree with os.walk(), shown by a program that renames every file to upper case; the zipfile module, with ZipFile objects in write, append and read use, namelist(), getinfo() with file_size and compress_size, extractall() and extract(); Project 5, backup_to_zip.py, which writes a folder into a ZIP file whose name counts up; and it closes with a summary, 4 practice questions and 4 practice programs: selective copying, finding large files, renumbering files and converting American to European dates.

The chapter's printed outputs reproduce under Python 3.14.4 except one sentence: shutil.copy() returned a str when the destination was a folder and a PosixPath when it was a file name, which is what the chapter prints; the walk of the chapter gave the same folders and files on each pass, but the documentation says that the order of names depends on the file system, so the chapter's listing is one possible order and the runs here sorted the names; the ZIP listing reproduced the member name file1.txt, file_size 50000, compress_size 97 and Compressed file is 515.46x smaller!, while the chapter's prose puts the compressed size at about 213 bytes, a number that neither compresslevel 9 nor the default level 6 gave (both 97; level 1 gave 293 and level 0 gave 50010), so the prose and the listing disagree with each other and only the listing runs.

The chapter says that a file1.txt already in the destination folder of shutil.move() would be overwritten; under Python 3.14.4 shutil.move() into a folder that already held file1.txt raised shutil.Error and moved nothing, which is what the documentation states (the destination path in the folder must not already exist), whereas a move onto an existing path that is not a folder replaced the file; the chapter also describes the return value of shutil.move() as a string, and it was a str for a folder destination and a PosixPath for a new file name.

The chapter's Project 5 program differs from what its prose intends in four ways that were run: write() without a compression type stores the file, so the snapshot is not compressed although the chapter speaks of compressing; passing absolute paths to write() stores the whole path of each file without its leading slash as the member name; giving the folder as Path('.') raises IndexError, because Path('.').parts is an empty tuple; and when the archive is created inside the folder being backed up, os.walk lists the archive and the program writes it into itself; the program also tests names in the working directory and not next to the folder.

The chapter's advice on deletion holds: os.unlink() deletes a file for good, os.rmdir() only an empty folder (OSError otherwise) and shutil.rmtree() a whole tree, and the dry run, in which the delete is replaced by a print, exposed the typo *.rxt for *.txt by matching no file; current Python adds that unlink() on a folder raises IsADirectoryError on this Linux system, that rmtree() on a missing path raises FileNotFoundError unless ignore_errors=True, and that the onexc parameter, added in Python 3.12, replaces the deprecated onerror as the way to handle errors while deleting a tree; send2trash was not executed.

For an advanced course, chapter 11 is best taught by asking of each operation whether it can be undone, whether it stays inside the folder it was given, and whether the program can show what it will do before it does it: copy and copytree keep the source and move does not, rmtree, unlink and rmdir cannot be undone and send2trash can; the chapter's outputs hold under 3.14.4 except the overwrite claim for shutil.move and the 213-byte sentence, and Project 5 needs its compression type, its archive names, its folder argument and the place of its archive fixed, while pathlib's walk, copy and move, the exclusive and append modes, make_archive and the safety of extraction are what the chapter leaves for the course to add.

Current Python gives file handling more than the chapter presents: shutil.copy2() keeps metadata such as the modification time and copytree() uses it, copytree(dirs_exist_ok=True) copies into an existing folder, Path objects are accepted by the shutil and os functions since PEP 519 and have iterdir(), glob() and rglob(), Path.walk() since Python 3.12 is os.walk() for Path objects, and since Python 3.14 Path.copy(), copy_into(), move() and move_into() copy and move without shutil.

Current Python gives archives more than the chapter presents: ZipFile mode 'x' refuses to overwrite and 'a' adds, ZipFile.mkdir() since Python 3.11 adds a folder entry, compression methods beyond deflate include ZIP_BZIP2, ZIP_LZMA and, new in Python 3.14, ZIP_ZSTANDARD, shutil.make_archive() and shutil.unpack_archive() do in one call what the chapter does with a program, extraction removes .. and leading slashes from member names so that the members of a hostile archive stay inside the target folder, and the documentation still warns never to extract untrusted archives without inspection.

nodes.label: Copying and moving
nodes.body: Copying, moving and renaming files and folders with the shutil module is the first subject of chapter 11, and every one of its functions takes a source and a destination and leaves the destination holding the content, by one path or another (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Copying, moving and renaming files and folders with the shutil module is the first subject of chapter 11, and every one of its functions takes a source and a destination and leaves the destination holding the content, by one path or another (Sweigart, 2025).

Two ideas carry the branch. Copying covers shutil.copy for one file and shutil.copytree for a whole folder, together with the metadata a plain copy loses and the dirs_exist_ok argument that lets a copy continue into a folder that is already there. Moving covers shutil.move, which both relocates and renames depending on its destination, the pathlib methods Python 3.14 added for the identical job, and what happens when the destination already holds a file of that name, the one place this branch's own chapter prose and its own listed behaviour part ways.

nodes.label: Copying
nodes.body: Two functions copy: shutil.copy for one file and shutil.copytree for a folder with everything in it, and both return the path they wrote to rather than nothing at all (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Two functions copy: shutil.copy for one file and shutil.copytree for a folder with everything in it, and both return the path they wrote to rather than nothing at all (Sweigart, 2025).

Copy file covers the plain, one-file case. Copy folder tree covers the whole-folder case, which needs a destination that is not already there. Copy with metadata is not in the chapter at all; it names the sibling function, shutil.copy2, that copytree itself actually calls underneath. Existing destination covers the dirs_exist_ok argument that lifts copytree's own one restriction.

nodes.label: Copy file
nodes.body: shutil.copy(source, destination) copies a file to a folder, which keeps the name, or to a file name, which becomes the copy's name (Sweigart, 2025); run under Python 3.14.6, copying a.txt into a folder named box and separately to b.txt inside that folder left a.txt, b.txt and the untouched source all in place, and the documentation adds that an existing destination file is replaced and that permission bits travel with the copy while other metadata does not (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: shutil.copy(source, destination) copies a file to a folder, which keeps the name, or to a file name, which becomes the copy's name (Sweigart, 2025); run under Python 3.14.6, copying a.txt into a folder named box and separately to b.txt inside that folder left a.txt, b.txt and the untouched source all in place, and the documentation adds that an existing destination file is replaced and that permission bits travel with the copy while other metadata does not (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Copy with metadata is the other function that fills in exactly the metadata a plain copy leaves behind, and copy folder tree is built from this same one-file copy repeated down a tree. Delete file is the operation that undoes what this one builds, permanently and with no copy left over once it runs, which is why safer deletion's own dry run is advised before either a delete or a copy that could overwrite something unseen.

nodes.definition: shutil.copy copies one file to a destination that is either a folder, which keeps the file's name, or a file name, which becomes the copy's name; an existing destination file is replaced, and the call returns the path of the new file.

nodes.label: Existing destination
nodes.body: The chapter's own copytree needs a destination that does not exist (Sweigart, 2025); since Python 3.8 dirs_exist_ok=True lets it continue into an existing folder instead, where a file of the same name already there is overwritten and every other file is left alone, so a destination folder whose a.txt read 'old' and whose keep.txt read 'kept' ended the call holding a.txt changed to 'new' and keep.txt untouched (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter's own copytree needs a destination that does not exist (Sweigart, 2025); since Python 3.8 dirs_exist_ok=True lets it continue into an existing folder instead, where a file of the same name already there is overwritten and every other file is left alone, so a destination folder whose a.txt read 'old' and whose keep.txt read 'kept' ended the call holding a.txt changed to 'new' and keep.txt untouched (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Copy folder tree names the one restriction this argument lifts. Move collision is the branch's other existing-destination case, and the two do not behave alike at all: copytree's dirs_exist_ok quietly overwrites a same-named file, while shutil.move into a folder that already holds that name refuses outright, a contrast worth holding side by side rather than assuming one implies the other.

nodes.definition: With dirs_exist_ok=True, copytree continues into a destination folder that already exists and overwrites files of the same name there, leaving the other files in place.

nodes.label: Moving
nodes.body: shutil.move moves and renames, and the chapter treats the two as one operation, decided entirely by what the destination argument turns out to be (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: shutil.move moves and renames, and the chapter treats the two as one operation, decided entirely by what the destination argument turns out to be (Sweigart, 2025).

Move file or folder covers the case where the destination is a folder that receives the source under its own name. Move as rename covers the case where it is not, so the call renames in place. Move collision covers what happens when a name collision cannot be avoided, the one place this chapter's own prose and its own executed behaviour disagree outright. Pathlib copy move closes the branch with the newer, shutil-free way Python 3.14 added to do the identical two jobs.

stories.title: The ZIP format was given away free on 14 February 1989
stories.who: Phil Katz, with Gary Conway of Infinity Design Concepts
stories.story: Phil Katz had already been sued by Systems Enhancement Associates, which claimed his own PKARC archiver copied its ARC format too closely; rather than fight over one more compatible format, Katz and Gary Conway of Infinity Design Concepts designed a new one of their own and, on 14 February 1989, PKWARE and Infinity Design Concepts issued a joint press release placing the .ZIP format in the public domain, free for any program to read or write. Katz's friend Robert Mahoney suggested the name itself, 'zip', meaning to move at high speed, to promise a program faster than ARC; the first specification, APPNOTE.TXT, shipped that same year inside Katz's own PKZIP 0.9. Every zipfile.ZipFile this chapter opens, in mode 'w', 'a' or 'r', reads and writes exactly the public-domain structure that one press release described.
stories.lesson: zipfile reads the format PKWARE gave away free on 14 Feb 1989
stories.source: 'ZIP (file format)', Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZIP_(file_format) (Phil Katz and Gary Conway, PKWARE and Infinity Design Concepts, public-domain press release 14 February 1989; APPNOTE.TXT first published in PKZIP 0.9, 1989). Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

stories.title: The compression under ZIP_DEFLATED shipped free on 1 May 1995
stories.where: the Free Software Foundation's own GNU project, by email
stories.story: Jean-Loup Gailly, who had already written the compression half of gzip, and Mark Adler, who wrote the matching decompression half, joined their work into a single free library they called zlib, built first for Thomas Boutell's own libpng image library rather than for any archiver at all. Gailly handled compressing and Adler handled decompressing, and together they released zlib 0.9 on 1 May 1995, a clean-room implementation of the DEFLATE algorithm that owed nothing to Phil Katz's own patented code, free of charge and free to embed in any program at all. Python's own zipfile module links against exactly this library whenever a write names compress_type=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED, the method this chapter's own backup project never actually asks for.
stories.lesson: ZIP_DEFLATED runs zlib, free since Gailly and Adler's 1995 release
stories.source: 'Zlib', Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zlib (Jean-Loup Gailly and Mark Adler, version 0.9 released 1 May 1995, written first for the libpng library). Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

stories.title: The recycle bin's own icon is a 1983 Macintosh drawing
stories.who: Susan Kare, with Andy Hertzfeld's icon editor
stories.story: Susan Kare joined Apple in 1983 with no formal training in computer graphics at all, and was asked to draw the small pictures the first Macintosh would need for its own commands; working on a 32-by-32 pixel grid that lead software architect Andy Hertzfeld had proposed, she first blocked the squares out by hand on graph paper before redrawing each one electronically in an icon editor Hertzfeld built on the Macintosh prototype itself. Among the icons Kare drew that year was the trash can, the picture that shipped on the Macintosh's own desktop in 1984 and has stood for a reversible delete on a graphical desktop ever since. The third-party send2trash module this chapter names moves a file to exactly that bin instead of deleting it outright, the one operation of this whole chapter that can still be undone by a user's own hand.
stories.lesson: send2trash's bin is Kare's own 1983 Macintosh trash icon
stories.source: Jackie Mansky, 'How Susan Kare Designed User-Friendly Icons for the First Macintosh', Smithsonian Magazine, smithsonianmag.com (Kare joined Apple 1983; Macintosh released 1984; Andy Hertzfeld's 32x32 grid and icon editor). Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

stories.title: The folder tree os.walk visits is a 1965 Multics design
stories.story: R.C. Daley of MIT's Project MAC, with P.G. Neumann of Bell Labs, presented 'A General Purpose File System for Secondary Storage' at the 1965 Fall Joint Computer Conference, laying out Multics's own tree-structured file system, folders holding folders holding files, built for a system meant to be shared by many users and administered in pieces at once. Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie, together with Doug McIlroy and J.F. Ossanna, had all worked on Multics at Bell Labs before the project's own slow progress pushed Bell Labs out of it, and the small operating system the four built next, Unix, kept the identical tree of folders inside folders at its very core. Every folder os.walk visits today, descending from one folder into its own subfolders in turn, walks the same shape Daley and Neumann described in 1965, fifty-six years before this chapter's own program renamed a single file inside it.
stories.lesson: os.walk descends the folder tree Daley and Neumann designed in 1965
stories.source: 'Multics History', multicians.org/history.html (R.C. Daley and P.G. Neumann, 'A General Purpose File System for Secondary Storage', Fall Joint Computer Conference, 1965; Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie and colleagues carried the tree into Unix after working on Multics). Photo: Wikimedia Commons.
